back2basics.concept: RBI's Regulatory Powers over Banks and NBFCs
back2basics.text: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the central banking authority responsible for regulating banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) in India. It issues Certificates of Registration to NBFCs allowing them to operate. RBI can cancel these certificates if the NBFC fails to comply with regulations. For banks, RBI can supersede the Board of Directors if governance or operational issues threaten the bank's stability. These powers help maintain financial stability and protect depositors.

2026-11-10-am-9b83c58bda.deck: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) cancelled the Certificate of Registration of Gandhinagar Leasing and Finance Ltd. on October 29, 2026, stopping it from operating as a Non-Banking Financial Institution. Simultaneously, RBI extended the supersession of the Board of Directors of Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank Ltd., Mumbai, for another year from November 24, 2026, due to ongoing governance concerns.

body.label: Cancellation of Gandhinagar Leasing
body.text: RBI cancelled the Certificate of Registration of Gandhinagar Leasing and Finance Ltd. on October 29, 2026, under Section 45-IA(6) of the RBI Act, 1934, prohibiting it from transacting as a Non-Banking Financial Institution.

body.label: Extension of Abhyudaya Bank board supersession
body.text: RBI extended the supersession of the Board of Directors of Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank Ltd. for one more year from November 24, 2026, citing material concerns over poor governance standards.

body.label: Administrator and advisors continued
body.text: Shri Satya Prakash Pathak continues as Administrator of Abhyudaya Bank, assisted by the Committee of Advisors comprising Shri Venkatesh Hegde, Shri Devendra Kumar, and Shri Suhas Gokhale.

sections.heading: What actions did the RBI take regarding Gandhinagar Leasing and Abhyudaya Bank?

body.label: Regulatory authority
body.text: RBI exercises its powers under the Reserve Bank of India Act and Banking Regulation Act to regulate NBFCs and banks to ensure financial stability and protect depositors.

body.label: Addressing governance issues
body.text: Supersession of a bank’s board occurs when RBI identifies material concerns such as poor governance standards that could threaten the bank’s sound functioning.

body.label: Public interest safeguard
body.text: Such regulatory actions are taken in the public interest to maintain trust in the financial system and prevent risks to depositors and the economy.

sections.heading: Why does RBI cancel registrations and supersede bank boards?

body.label: Understanding RBI’s regulatory role
body.text: These actions exemplify RBI’s statutory powers to regulate NBFCs and cooperative banks, relevant for questions on financial regulation and governance.

body.label: Banking governance and reforms
body.text: The extension of board supersession highlights challenges in governance in cooperative banks and RBI’s intervention mechanisms.

body.label: Legal provisions invoked
body.text: Sections 45-IA(6) of the RBI Act and Section 36AAA read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act are key legal provisions governing these actions.

back2basics.text: PMEGP is a central government scheme aimed at generating employment by providing financial assistance to micro-enterprises. It involves bank loans and subsidies to beneficiaries to start or expand businesses. Effective monitoring is essential to prevent misuse and ensure the scheme benefits intended recipients.

2026-11-10-am-ed7b965be9.deck: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) attached immovable properties worth ₹10.63 crore in Jammu and Kashmir for alleged misuse of the Prime Minister Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) loans. This case highlights governance and accountability challenges in the implementation of central welfare schemes.

mcq.stem:
Consider the following statements about the PMEGP misuse case in Kashmir:
1. The ED attached immovable properties worth ₹10.63 crore under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.
2. The misappropriation involved fake borrowers, bank officials from J&K Bank, and brokers.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
mcq.trap: Both statements are correct; a trap would be confusing the role of the ED with other agencies or misquoting the property value.

body.label: Property attachment
body.text: The ED attached immovable properties worth ₹10.63 crore under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act in connection with alleged misuse of PMEGP loans.

body.label: Misappropriation details
body.text: Loans under the PMEGP scheme were misappropriated through a criminal conspiracy involving fake borrowers, fake invoices of non-existent firms, bank officials from Sumbal and Gamud Gadkhud branches of J&K Bank, and private brokers.

body.label: Diversion of funds
body.text: The proceeds from the offences were diverted through multiple bank transactions and partly used for asset construction, renovation, and personal enrichment.

body.label: Investigation status
body.text: The ED traced proceeds of crime amounting to ₹11.37 crore and investigations are ongoing; the CBI and J&K Anti-Corruption Bureau also registered cases in June 2026.

body.text: Misuse of PMEGP loans undermines the scheme’s goal of promoting employment and entrepreneurship among the youth.

body.label: Accountability challenges
body.text: The involvement of bank officials and brokers in the conspiracy reveals gaps in monitoring and accountability in scheme implementation.

body.label: Anti-corruption enforcement
body.text: The ED’s action under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act demonstrates the government’s efforts to curb financial crimes linked to welfare schemes.
